contributions.headingText: Cowden syndrome (CS) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by multiple hamartomas involving organs derived from any of the three germ layers, with cancer predisposition.

Acceptable: Cowden disease; multiple hamartoma syndrome; PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome.

PTEN hamartoma tumour syndrome (PHTS) is a heterogeneous group of disorders with autosomal dominant inheritance, caused by germline mutation of the PTEN gene. PHTS also includes Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome and Proteus syndrome. However, most cases of PHTS correspond to CS, and the terms “PHTS” and “CS” are often used interchangeably {19668082}.

Gastrointestinal polyps are present in virtually all patients with CS, occurring throughout the GI tract. Diffuse oesophageal glycogenic acanthosis is present in > 80% of CS cases. CS is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer {6496844; 21437855; 23238744}.

CS is characterized by mucocutaneous lesions (multiple facial trichilemmomas, acral keratoses, papillomatous papules, and mucosal lesions are considered pathognomonic), an increased cancer risk, benign hamartomatous overgrowth of tissues (including gastrointestinal polyposis), and macrocephaly (see Box #0120 and Table #0121) {24136893}. Cancer risk is relatively broad, with risk of breast, thyroid, endometrial, renal cell, and colon cancers; melanoma; and other cancers {20301661}.
The prevalence is estimated at about 1 in 200 000–250 000 in European populations, but this may be an underestimate, given the difficulty in diagnosing this syndrome {10234502}.

CS is an autosomal dominant disorder with age-related penetrance and variable expression. Germline mutation in PTEN (10q23.3) is found in about 85% of CS cases, as well as in subsets of other PHTS disorders (in 65% of Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome cases, 20% of Proteus syndrome cases, and 50% of Proteus-like syndrome cases) {19668082; 18794875; 9140396; 8673088}. Individualized risk calculation may aid assessment of a patient’s risk of carrying a germline PTEN mutation based on clinical features {21194675}.

Germline succinate dehydrogenase mutations have been found in about 5% of PTEN mutation–negative CS / CS-like individuals and are associated with increased frequencies of breast, thyroid, and renal cancers beyond those conferred by germline PTEN mutation {18678321}.

PTEN is a virtually ubiquitously expressed tumour suppressor and a dual-specificity lipid and protein phosphatase that regulates cell proliferation, cell migration, and apoptosis through inhibition of AKT via the PI3K/AKT pathway {23613428}. Inactivation of the second copy of the gene allows deregulation of the AKT pathway.
See the descriptions of the polyps within the relevant sections.

Gastrointestinal polyps in CS represent a mixture of histology {20600018}. Hyperplastic polyps, hamartomatous/juvenile polyps, adenomas, and ganglioneuromas are the most frequent types of polyps in the colon {26721304}. Polyps typically measure between 3–10 mm, but they can be larger. Hyperplastic polyps are not part of the diagnostic criteria for PHTS. Colonic intramucosal lipomas have also been associated with CS {29192650}.

Polyps in the duodenum are mainly hamartomas and some ganglioneuromas and adenomas {26721304}. Most patients with CS have gastric polyps {21437855; 23238744}, which are usually numerous, measure 1–20 mm, and are mostly diagnosed as hyperplastic or hamartomatous polyps. Dysplasia has not been reported in gastric CS polyps. Although incidental CS patients with gastric cancer have been reported, an increased gastric cancer risk has not been verified {20600018; 22252256; 26721304}. Diffuse oesophageal glycogenic acanthosis in combination with colonic polyposis may be diagnostic of CS {21437855; 23238744}.
The International Cowden Consortium (ICC) operational diagnostic criteria are listed in Box #0120.
Patients with PHTS are at increased risk of several types of cancer, and interval screening is recommended (see Table #0121) {22252256; 23613428; 23335809}.
